title: Practical Federated Recommendation Model Learning Using ORAM with Controlled Privacy
problem: Federated learning (FL) for recommendation models is impractical because the large embedding tables require each user to access a tiny fraction of table entries, and hiding those access patterns via ORAM incurs prohibitive latency and SSD wear. Existing ORAM-based approaches have latency and SSD lifetime overheads that make them undeployable at scale.
method: FEDORA places the large ORAM structure on SSDs rather than DRAM, using SSD-friendly access optimizations to reduce write amplification and wear. It introduces epsilon-FDP (Federated Differential Privacy), a formal framework that trades off ORAM privacy strength against performance by allowing a controlled, quantified privacy budget, reducing the number of ORAM operations required. The system also supports modern FL operation modes (e.g., asynchronous and partial participation) so it integrates with production FL pipelines.

title: Hydra: Scale-out FHE Accelerator Architecture for Secure Deep Learning on FPGA
problem: Existing FHE accelerators for deep learning focus on single-node throughput by stacking parallelized compute clusters, which cannot leverage application-level parallelism across model layers and are not scalable beyond a single card for increasingly large models.
method: Hydra partitions the deep learning model (CNN and LLM layers) across multiple FPGA-based server nodes, each handling a portion of the model governed by a central scheduling mechanism on the host server. The architecture supports multi-server scaling with theoretically arbitrary numbers of compute nodes, enabling pipeline parallelism at the model level in addition to intra-node parallelism. Hydra achieves scale-out by distributing ciphertext operations across nodes with the host managing data routing and synchronization.

title: TaOPT: Tool-Agnostic Optimization of Parallelized Automated Mobile UI Testing
problem: Parallelizing automated mobile UI testing across multiple test devices is inefficient because existing tools explore overlapping UI subspaces on different devices, wasting resources by redundantly testing similar app states. No existing approach optimizes the parallelization of arbitrary automated UI testing tools without modifying their internal workflow.
method: TaOPT performs online UI subspace inference by analyzing the App Under Test (AUT) to identify loosely coupled UI subspaces—regions of the app's state graph that can be explored independently. TaOPT then coordinates access to these subspaces across different testing devices, guiding each device's testing tool toward distinct, unexplored subspaces without modifying the tool's internal search logic (tool-agnostic). This subspace partitioning and assignment is updated dynamically as testing progresses, using observations of which subspaces each device has covered to avoid redundancy. By separating exploration across devices at the subspace granularity, TaOPT maximizes coverage diversity.

title: FALA: Locality-Aware PIM-Host Cooperation for Graph Processing with Fine-Grained Column Access
problem: Graph processing exhibits irregular memory access patterns that cause significant memory bandwidth waste on DRAM architectures: cache-based graph tiling suffers from overfetching due to the mismatch between DRAM burst size and the sparse data actually needed, while PIM-based approaches fail to exploit cache locality for high-reuse workloads.
method: FALA is a hybrid architecture integrating PIM and cache-based acceleration. It introduces a fine-grained column access mechanism within DRAM memory banks that allows selective access to individual columns (vertices) rather than fetching full DRAM rows, eliminating overfetching for sparse graph accesses. A locality-aware PIM architecture is designed to route accesses: high-reuse vertex data is served through the host CPU cache hierarchy, while low-reuse, irregular accesses are processed near-memory via PIM. The design minimizes unnecessary memory traffic while fully utilizing both internal DRAM bandwidth and on-chip caches.

title: Extended User Interrupts (xUI): Fast and Flexible Notification without Polling
problem: Intel's existing User Interrupt (UIPI) mechanism for fast user-space notification has correctness and performance limitations that prevent it from matching shared-memory polling latency while maintaining the efficiency of asynchronous notification. Current designs lack support for preemption in user-level runtimes, kernel-bypass timers, and efficient interrupt forwarding to accelerators.
method: xUI extends Intel's UIPI model with four hardware mechanisms: (1) tracked interrupts that allow senders to know when an interrupt was delivered, (2) hardware safepoints that let user-level runtimes implement preemption without kernel involvement, (3) a kernel-bypass timer for deadline-driven scheduling, and (4) interrupt forwarding to route notifications directly to accelerators (modeled on Intel's DSA). The design is modeled and evaluated in gem5 full-system simulation, measuring end-to-end latency for three distinct use cases.

title: Misam: Machine Learning Assisted Dataflow Selection in Accelerators for Sparse Matrix Multiplication
problem: SpGEMM accelerators that support multiple dataflows (e.g., row-wise, column-wise, inner-product) face two critical problems: (1) no fast principled mechanism exists for selecting the optimal dataflow at runtime given input matrix sparsity patterns, and (2) providing hardware flexibility for multiple dataflows incurs area overhead and underutilization when one dataflow is locked in.
method: Misam uses a lightweight decision tree classifier to dynamically predict the optimal SpGEMM hardware configuration from matrix structural features (sparsity density, distribution, pattern statistics) extracted at runtime. To overcome hardware underutilization from multi-dataflow support, Misam targets FPGAs and exploits FPGA partial reconfigurability to deploy specialized, resource-efficient bitstreams tailored to specific sparsity regimes on demand. A reconfiguration engine evaluates whether the anticipated performance gain from switching bitstreams exceeds the reconfiguration overhead before triggering a reconfiguration.

title: REIS: A High-Performance and Energy-Efficient Retrieval System with In-Storage Processing
problem: The retrieval stage of RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) is a throughput bottleneck because Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search (ANNS) on large embedding databases incurs massive data movement between host and storage; existing In-Storage Processing (ISP) approaches use storage-agnostic ANNS algorithms, do not accelerate the subsequent data-fetch step, and require heavy SSD hardware modifications.
method: REIS co-designs the ANNS algorithm with ISP hardware inside the storage system to avoid host-storage data movement. It adopts an ISP-tailored ANNS algorithm that exploits the internal bandwidth and parallelism of NAND flash controllers without large hardware modifications. REIS additionally accelerates the data-retrieval step for items selected by ANNS, overlapping fetch and search computations. The system is designed to minimize changes to storage hardware while maximizing throughput.

title: PowerMove: Optimizing Compilation for Neutral Atom Quantum Computers with Zoned Architecture
problem: Neutral atom quantum computers (NAQCs) with zoned architectures (ZA) and qubit movement capabilities require coordinated gate scheduling, qubit positioning, atom movement, and inter-zone communication, but existing compilers cannot jointly optimize these dimensions, leading to poor fidelity and long execution times for quantum circuits.
method: PowerMove is a compiler for NAQCs that jointly optimizes gate scheduling, qubit positioning, atom movement, and inter-zone communication for zoned architectures. The compiler introduces new optimization passes that model atom movement as a first-class resource and explore movement strategies jointly with gate ordering. For NISQ applications, PowerMove significantly reduces the number of atom movements and inter-zone communications, while for FTQC (fault-tolerant quantum computing), it replaces physical qubits with logical qubits encoded in quantum error correction (QEC) codes and applies analogous optimization. The compilation algorithm is designed for both correctness and efficiency, achieving up to 216.9x compilation speedup over prior methods.

title: pulse: Accelerating Distributed Pointer-Traversals on Disaggregated Memory
problem: CPU-side caches in disaggregated memory architectures cannot amortize network latency for pointer-chasing workloads over linked data structures, because each traversal step depends on the preceding one, making prefetching and caching ineffective.
method: pulse is a distributed pointer-traversal framework that executes pointer-chasing computations close to disaggregated memory rather than at CPU nodes. Traversal kernels are offloaded to processing elements co-located with memory, supporting various linked data structures with a programmable traversal interface. The framework supports distributed execution across multiple memory nodes for rack-scale workloads, preserving expressiveness while improving latency, throughput, and energy efficiency relative to cache-based access.

title: Aqua: Network-Accelerated Memory Offloading for LLMs in Scale-Up GPU Domains
problem: LLM inference under bursty request patterns exhausts GPU memory, causing serving engines to use admission control that renders them unresponsive; preemptive time-sliced scheduling requires KV-cache paging that incurs high overhead and reduces throughput.
method: Aqua is a GPU memory management framework that uses the high-bandwidth scale-up network (NVLink/NVSwitch fabric within a server) as a fast memory offloading path for paging LLM inference state (KV caches). When a prompt is preempted, Aqua pages its KV cache over the scale-up network to remote GPU memory on other nodes rather than to slow host DRAM or NVMe, dramatically reducing paging latency. A scheduling layer enables preemptive time-sliced prompt execution on top of this low-overhead paging mechanism.

title: Chimera: Communication Fusion for Hybrid Parallelism in Large Language Models
problem: Hybrid parallelism strategies (tensor, pipeline, sequence, data parallelism combined) for LLM training and inference on multi-NPU systems generate a large volume of diverse collective communications whose blocking nature severely throttles compute utilization. Redundant communication operators introduced by combining multiple parallelism dimensions compound this bottleneck.
method: Chimera performs a systematic analysis of communication processes for each parallelism dimension (tensor, pipeline, data, sequence), identifies redundant collective operations that arise when multiple parallelism strategies are combined, and eliminates them by fusing adjacent communication operators during parallelism transformation. It reorders operations and generates a single redundancy-free communication operator that achieves the semantics of the original multi-collective sequence. The resulting fused operator is injected into the LLM computation graph as a replacement for the original blocking collectives.

title: OptiPIM: Optimizing Processing-in-Memory Acceleration Using Integer Linear Programming
problem: Efficient PIM acceleration requires precise software-hardware mapping that transforms application algorithms into PIM operations and data layouts, but existing PIM accelerators rely on manually tuned heuristics or exhaustive search, producing under-optimized mappings and/or prohibitively long optimization times.
method: OptiPIM formulates the PIM mapping problem as an Integer Linear Programming (ILP) problem using a PIM-friendly mapping representation with accurate cost modeling that concisely covers the entire design space. The framework is implemented as a compiler pass inside the open-source MLIR framework, enabling it to consume PyTorch workloads and emit optimized mappings for PIM accelerators. OptiPIM generates optimal mappings within 4 minutes by exploiting the problem structure to make the ILP tractable.

title: AiF: Accelerating On-Device LLM Inference Using In-Flash Processing
problem: On-device LLM inference with SSD offloading is severely bottlenecked by the limited external read bandwidth of flash storage (NAND-to-host path), making inference latency unacceptably high even though LLM weight matrices fit in flash capacity. Existing SSD offloading engines are bound by PCIe/interface bandwidth rather than the high internal NAND bandwidth.
method: AiF integrates matrix-vector multiplication (GEMV) compute units directly inside flash chips (Accelerator-in-Flash), exploiting the high internal NAND plane-level bandwidth without routing data across the external interface. Two novel flash read techniques are introduced specifically for LLM weight access patterns stored in flash memory. AiF also employs a streamlined error correction process that delivers a 4x boost in internal read bandwidth with minimal overhead, enabling in-flash GEMV operations to run at near-full internal bandwidth.

title: Ariadne: A Hotness-Aware and Size-Adaptive Compressed Swap Technique for Fast Application Relaunch and Reduced CPU Usage on Mobile Devices
problem: Mobile devices under memory pressure use ZRAM (RAM-based compressed swap) to defer app eviction, but ZRAM prolongs relaunch latency and wastes CPU time because it applies uniform compression settings regardless of data hotness, does not differentiate compression chunk size, and lacks prefetching of soon-to-be-needed decompressed data.
method: Ariadne introduces three coordinated techniques: (1) a low-overhead hotness-aware data organization scheme that classifies anonymous memory pages as hot, warm, or cold based on observed relaunch access patterns, allowing reuse of hotness labels across consecutive relaunches; (2) a size-adaptive compression scheme that uses small chunk sizes for hot/warm data (enabling fast decompression on the critical relaunch path) and large chunk sizes for cold data (improving compression ratio); and (3) a proactive decompression scheme that predicts the next set of pages needed during relaunch and decompresses them in advance to overlap decompression with computation.

title: Panacea: Novel DNN Accelerator using Accuracy-Preserving Asymmetric Quantization and Energy-Saving Bit-Slice Sparsity
problem: Symmetric quantization introduces unacceptable accuracy loss for large-scale DNNs due to asymmetric activation distributions, but existing asymmetric quantization schemes produce many nonzero bit-slices that cannot be exploited by bit-slice GEMM accelerators designed for symmetric (zero-heavy) representations.
method: Panacea introduces Asymmetrically-Quantized bit-Slice GEMM (AQS-GEMM), which compresses frequent nonzero slices generated by asymmetric quantization and skips their computation. Two algorithm-hardware co-optimization techniques increase slice-level sparsity: zero-point manipulation (adjusting quantization zero points to shift frequent values toward zero) and distribution-based bit-slicing (selecting bit-slices that maximize sparsity based on activation distribution). Panacea's dataflow is specialized for sparse/dense mixed workloads on tiled AQS-GEMM, with run-length encoding to maximize data reuse and minimize off-chip memory traffic.

title: Caravan: A Hardware/Software Co-Design for Efficient SIMD Neighbor Search on Point Clouds
problem: Neighbor search in 3D point cloud processing via k-d trees is compute-intensive and exhibits SIMD underutilization: consecutive queries follow similar tree paths but diverge at deeper levels, causing sparse VPU lane usage that standard SIMD instructions cannot efficiently handle.
method: Caravan-SW batches consecutive neighbor search queries that visit similar k-d tree nodes and processes them in parallel using SIMD (AVX512) instructions. At deeper tree levels where query navigation diverges, Caravan-HW adds two new ISA instructions that enable re-indexing of valid (non-empty) SIMD lanes and fast operand shuffling, allowing dense SIMD operations on the remaining active lanes. The hardware modification is lightweight, requiring only 0.032 mm2 of additional silicon area.
